claim: The origin of the insect odorant receptor (OR) gene family has been hypothesized to have coincided with the evolution of terrestriality in insects.
source: The origin of the insect odorant receptor (OR) gene family has been hypothesized to have coincided with the evolution of terrestriality in insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robertson et al., 2003, as stated later in the manuscript.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) suggested that ORs evolved with an ancestral OR co-receptor (Orco) after the origin of terrestriality and the OR/Orco system is an adaptation to winged flight in insects.
source: Missbach et al. (2014) suggested that ORs instead evolved with an ancestral OR co-receptor (Orco) after the origin of terrestriality and the OR/Orco system is an adaptation to winged flight in insects.
evidence: This claim is attributed to Missbach et al. (2014) through citation.

claim: ORs are present in all insect genomes investigated.
source: We investigated genomes of the Collembola, Diplura, Archaeognatha, Zygentoma, Odonata, and Ephemeroptera, and find ORs present in all insect genomes but absent from lineages predating the evolution of insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis of multiple insect orders.

claim: ORs are absent from lineages predating the evolution of insects.
source: We investigated genomes of the Collembola, Diplura, Archaeognatha, Zygentoma, Odonata, and Ephemeroptera, and find ORs present in all insect genomes but absent from lineages predating the evolution of insects.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis showing no ORs in Collembola and Diplura.

claim: Orco is absent only in the ancestrally wingless insect lineage Archaeognatha.
source: Orco is absent only in the ancestrally wingless insect lineage Archaeognatha.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis of Archaeognatha.

claim: The zygentoman firebrat Thermobia domestica has a full OR/Orco system.
source: Our new genome sequence of the zygentoman firebrat Thermobia domestica reveals a full OR/Orco system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome sequencing and annotation of T. domestica.

claim: ORs evolved before winged flight.
source: We conclude that ORs evolved before winged flight, perhaps as an adaptation to terrestriality, representing a key evolutionary novelty in the ancestor of all insects, and hence a molecular synapomorphy for the Class Insecta.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in wingless insects (Archaeognatha and Zygentoma).

claim: ORs represent a key evolutionary novelty in the ancestor of all insects.
source: We conclude that ORs evolved before winged flight, perhaps as an adaptation to terrestriality, representing a key evolutionary novelty in the ancestor of all insects, and hence a molecular synapomorphy for the Class Insecta.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: ORs are a molecular synapomorphy for the Class Insecta.
source: We conclude that ORs evolved before winged flight, perhaps as an adaptation to terrestriality, representing a key evolutionary novelty in the ancestor of all insects, and hence a molecular synapomorphy for the Class Insecta.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: Living organisms of all levels of complexity have evolved chemosensory receptors to detect and discriminate chemicals in the environment.
source: From bacteria to mammals, living organisms of all levels of complexity have evolved chemosensory receptors to detect and discriminate chemicals in the environment (Wuichet and Zhulin, 2010; Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wuichet and Zhulin, 2010 and Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011.

claim: The largest metazoan gene families encode tens to hundreds of odorant receptors (ORs) that interact with volatile chemicals at the sensory periphery underlying the sense of smell.
source: The largest metazoan gene families encode tens to hundreds of odorant receptors (ORs) that interact with volatile chemicals at the sensory periphery underlying the sense of smell (Sánchez-Gracia et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sánchez-Gracia et al., 2009.

claim: OR gene families have evolved multiple times throughout the metazoans, including independent origins in vertebrates, nematodes, and insects.
source: OR gene families have evolved multiple times throughout the metazoans, including independent origins in vertebrates, nematodes, and insects (Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hansson and Stensmyr, 2011.

claim: In insects, the OR gene family evolved from within the ancestral gustatory receptor (GR) gene family.
source: In insects, the OR gene family evolved from within the ancestral gustatory receptor (GR) gene family (Scott et al., 2001; Robertson et al., 2003) that extends back to ancient metazoan lineages (Robertson, 2015; Saina et al., 2015; Eyun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 2001 and Robertson et al., 2003.

claim: The GR gene family extends back to ancient metazoan lineages.
source: In insects, the OR gene family evolved from within the ancestral gustatory receptor (GR) gene family (Scott et al., 2001; Robertson et al., 2003) that extends back to ancient metazoan lineages (Robertson, 2015; Saina et al., 2015; Eyun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Robertson, 2015; Saina et al., 2015; Eyun et al., 2017.

claim: ORs are absent from non-insect arthropod genomes.
source: ORs are absent from non-insect arthropod genomes (Peñalva-Arana et al., 2009; Almeida et al., 2015; Gulia-Nuss et al., 2016; Ngoc et al., 2016; Eyun et al., 2017), and have been hypothesized to have evolved concomitant with the evolution of terrestriality in insects (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ORs have been hypothesized to have evolved concomitant with the evolution of terrestriality in insects.
source: ORs are absent from non-insect arthropod genomes (Peñalva-Arana et al., 2009; Almeida et al., 2015; Gulia-Nuss et al., 2016; Ngoc et al., 2016; Eyun et al., 2017), and have been hypothesized to have evolved concomitant with the evolution of terrestriality in insects (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Robertson et al., 2003.

claim: ORs are absent in non-insect hexapods such as Collembola.
source: Only recently, whole-genome sequencing efforts suggested that ORs are absent in non-insect hexapods such as Collembola (Wu et al., 2017) but present in derived winged (pterygote) insects such as damselflies (Odonata; Ioannidis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: ORs are present in derived winged (pterygote) insects such as damselflies (Odonata).
source: Only recently, whole-genome sequencing efforts suggested that ORs are absent in non-insect hexapods such as Collembola (Wu et al., 2017) but present in derived winged (pterygote) insects such as damselflies (Odonata; Ioannidis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2017.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) identified three ORs in the firebrat Thermobia domestica, which they named TdomOrco1-3.
source: Efforts to understand more precisely the origin of the OR gene family within hexapods were greatly advanced by the findings of Missbach et al. (2014), who sequenced transcriptomes of the chemosensory organs of two apterygote insects, the bristletail Lepismachilis y-signata (Archaeognatha) and the firebrat Thermobia domestica (Zygentoma). They identified three ORs in the firebrat, which they named TdomOrco1-3, due to apparent similarity to the odorant receptor co-receptor (Orco; Vosshall and Hansson, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Missbach et al., 2014.

claim: Orco is a highly conserved single-copy gene present in all other insects studied to date.
source: Orco is a highly conserved single-copy gene present in all other insects studied to date and encodes a protein that is a partner with each of the other 'specific' ORs (Benton et al., 2006), a dimer required for OR-based olfaction in insects (Larsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Benton et al., 2006 and Larsson et al., 2004.

claim: Orco encodes a protein that is a partner with each of the other 'specific' ORs.
source: Orco is a highly conserved single-copy gene present in all other insects studied to date and encodes a protein that is a partner with each of the other 'specific' ORs (Benton et al., 2006), a dimer required for OR-based olfaction in insects (Larsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Benton et al., 2006.

claim: Orco forms a dimer required for OR-based olfaction in insects.
source: Orco is a highly conserved single-copy gene present in all other insects studied to date and encodes a protein that is a partner with each of the other 'specific' ORs (Benton et al., 2006), a dimer required for OR-based olfaction in insects (Larsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Larsson et al., 2004.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) could not find ORs or Orco relatives in their bristletail transcriptome.
source: In contrast, Missbach et al. (2014) could not find ORs or Orco relatives in their bristletail transcriptome, instead finding only members of the ionotropic receptor (IR) gene family.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Missbach et al., 2014.

claim: IRs serve olfactory roles in terrestrial crustaceans and insects.
source: Given evidence that IRs serve olfactory roles in terrestrial crustaceans and insects (Rytz et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rimal and Lee, 2018), they argued that olfaction in terrestrial non-insect hexapods and apterygote insects is entirely IR-dependent, with Orco evolving as ancestral OR from the GR lineage between the Archaeognatha and Zygentoma.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rytz et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rimal and Lee, 2018.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) argued that olfaction in terrestrial non-insect hexapods and apterygote insects is entirely IR-dependent.
source: Given evidence that IRs serve olfactory roles in terrestrial crustaceans and insects (Rytz et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rimal and Lee, 2018), they argued that olfaction in terrestrial non-insect hexapods and apterygote insects is entirely IR-dependent, with Orco evolving as ancestral OR from the GR lineage between the Archaeognatha and Zygentoma.
evidence: This claim is attributed to Missbach et al., 2014 through citation.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) suggested that Orco evolved as ancestral OR from the GR lineage between the Archaeognatha and Zygentoma.
source: Given evidence that IRs serve olfactory roles in terrestrial crustaceans and insects (Rytz et al., 2013; Groh-Lunow et al., 2014; Rimal and Lee, 2018), they argued that olfaction in terrestrial non-insect hexapods and apterygote insects is entirely IR-dependent, with Orco evolving as ancestral OR from the GR lineage between the Archaeognatha and Zygentoma.
evidence: This claim is attributed to Missbach et al., 2014 through citation.

claim: Missbach et al. (2014) suggested that the Orco/OR system evolved together with flight in pterygote insects.
source: Based on these findings, Missbach et al. (2014) suggested that the Orco/OR system evolved together with flight in pterygote insects and left off with the observation that 'the existence of three Orco types remains mysterious'.
evidence: This claim is attributed to Missbach et al., 2014 through citation.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis of the OR gene family of the damselfly Calopteryx splendens suggested that at least one of the three Orco-like ORs from T. domestica, TdomOrco3, might be a specific OR instead of an Orco.
source: Recently, phylogenetic analysis of the OR gene family of the damselfly Calopteryx splendens suggested that at least one of the three Orco-like ORs from T. domestica, TdomOrco3, might be a specific OR instead of an Orco (Ioannidis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2017.

claim: No ORs were detected in two non-insect hexapod lineages, Collembola and Diplura.
source: We detected no ORs in two non-insect hexapod lineages, Collembola and Diplura (a genome sequence is not available for the third lineage, the Protura), despite extensive annotation efforts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis.

claim: Genes with similarity to known insect ORs were identified in all insect genomes investigated.
source: In contrast, we identified genes with similarity to known insect ORs in all insect genomes investigated (Figure 1; Tables S2 and S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis and referenced in Figure 1 and supplementary tables.

claim: ORs were likely present in the ancestor of all insects but absent from all non-insect hexapod lineages.
source: Accordingly, ORs were likely present in the ancestor of all insects but absent from all non-insect hexapod lineages.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: The origin of the OR gene family coincided with the evolution of insects.
source: This suggests that the origin of the OR gene family coincided with the evolution of insects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: The analysis does not support the hypothesis that ORs evolved with the evolution of winged flight in insects.
source: Thus, our analysis does not support the hypothesis that ORs evolved with the evolution of winged flight in insects (Missbach et al., 2014) but is compatible with the hypothesis that they evolved with terrestriality in insects (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in wingless insects.

claim: The analysis is compatible with the hypothesis that ORs evolved with terrestriality in insects.
source: Thus, our analysis does not support the hypothesis that ORs evolved with the evolution of winged flight in insects (Missbach et al., 2014) but is compatible with the hypothesis that they evolved with terrestriality in insects (Robertson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: The T. domestica genome encodes 43 ORs encoded by 32 genes including the three previously identified genes (TdomOrco1-3).
source: We find that the T. domestica genome encodes far more than the three Orco-like OR proteins they described. Our manual annotation revealed 43 ORs encoded by 32 genes including the three previously identified genes (TdomOrco1-3; Missbach et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation of T. domestica.

claim: Four T. domestica OR genes are modeled as exhibiting alternative splicing leading to additional protein isoforms.
source: Four genes are modeled as exhibiting alternative splicing leading to the additional protein isoforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation of T. domestica.

claim: Only a few transcriptome reads mapped to the 'specific' OR genes in T. domestica.
source: We used the antennal transcriptome of Missbach et al. (2014) for support of intron-exon boundaries, however only a few transcriptome reads mapped to the 'specific' OR genes (Table S2 in Supplementary file 1), indicating that these ORs might be expressed in untested tissues or life stages, or at such low levels that the RNA-seq analysis of Missbach et al. (2014) did not sequence to a sufficient depth to recover these low-expressed transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: One of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of all ORs we annotated in the bristletail Machilis hrabei (5 ORs), the dragonfly Ladona fulva (4 ORs), and the mayfly Ephemera danica (47 ORs), as well as the previously annotated damselfly C. splendens (6 ORs; Ioannidis et al., 2017) revealed that one of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects (Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: TdomOrco2 shares unique features with the pterygote Orco proteins, such as a TKKQ motif in the expanded intracellular loop 2.
source: We believe this is the sole Orco relative because it shares unique features with the pterygote Orco proteins, such as a TKKQ motif in the expanded intracellular loop 2 (positions 327–330 in DmelOrco), and so we rename it simply TdomOrco.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis of TdomOrco2.

claim: TdomOr1-8 share a common gene structure with TdomOrco, with introns in phases 0-2-0-0-0.
source: TdomOr1-8 are a set of Orco-like proteins that share a common gene structure with TdomOrco, with introns in phases 0-2-0-0-0.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis of T. domestica ORs.

claim: The last four introns of TdomOr1-8 are present in all the other TdomOr genes, as well as those of the bristletail, odonates, and mayfly.
source: These last four introns are present in all the other TdomOr genes, as well as those of the bristletail, odonates, and mayfly, and correspond to the four introns identified by Robertson et al. (2003) as being ancestral to the OR family.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative gene structure analysis across species.

claim: The last four introns of TdomOr1-8 correspond to the four introns identified by Robertson et al. (2003) as being ancestral to the OR family.
source: These last four introns are present in all the other TdomOr genes, as well as those of the bristletail, odonates, and mayfly, and correspond to the four introns identified by Robertson et al. (2003) as being ancestral to the OR family.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to Robertson et al. (2003) findings.

claim: The first phase-0 intron of Orco and Or1-8 is the only additional intron shared by most pterygote Orco genes.
source: The first phase-0 intron of Orco and Or1-8 is the only additional intron shared by most pterygote Orco genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative gene structure analysis.

claim: All insect genomes analyzed have both single genes with high similarity to Orco and multiple genes with similarity to specific ORs, with the exception of the bristletail M. hrabei.
source: With the exception of the bristletail M. hrabei, all insect genomes analyzed have both single genes with high similarity to Orco and multiple genes with similarity to specific ORs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis across multiple insect species.

claim: The M. hrabei genome did not encode an Orco, but instead contains 5 ORs of high similarity that form a highly supported clade in the gene phylogeny.
source: The M. hrabei genome did not encode an Orco, but instead contains 5 ORs of high similarity that form a highly supported clade in the gene phylogeny (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: An Orco could not be found in the deep RNAseq transcriptome Missbach et al. (2014) generated for their bristletail, L. y-signata.
source: We also could not find an Orco in the deep RNAseq transcriptome Missbach et al. (2014) generated for their bristletail, L. y-signata.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of transcriptome data.

claim: Unsuccessful searches of raw reads from the M. hrabei genome project make it unlikely that M. hrabei has an Orco gene not present in the draft genome assembly due to an assembly gap.
source: While it is formally possible that M. hrabei has an Orco gene that is not present in the draft genome assembly due to an assembly gap, unsuccessful searches of raw reads from this genome project make this unlikely.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of raw sequencing reads.

claim: If bristletails lost their Orco gene, this loss must have occurred recently in both bristletail species because their 'specific' ORs are still intact.
source: First, bristletails might have lost their Orco gene, however this loss must have occurred recently in both bristletail species because their 'specific' ORs are still intact.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of intact specific ORs in bristletails.

claim: The OR family might have originated with a few specific ORs like those of M. hrabei, with the Orco lineage evolving between Archaegnatha and Zygentoma.
source: Second, the OR family might have originated with a few specific ORs like those of M. hrabei, with the Orco lineage evolving between Archaegnatha and Zygentoma.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the phylogenetic distribution of ORs and Orco.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis using various sets of GRs from other insects, arthropods, and animals as outgroup to root the OR family tree does not resolve the question of OR/Orco origin confidently.
source: Phylogenetic analysis using various sets of GRs from other insects, arthropods, and animals as outgroup to root the OR family tree does not resolve this question confidently (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' phylogenetic analyses.

claim: If functional, the five specific ORs in M. hrabei apparently function in the absence of Orco, perhaps alone or as dimers.
source: In any case, if indeed functional, these five specific ORs in M. hrabei, at least one of which is present in L. y-signata, apparently function in the absence of Orco, perhaps alone or as dimers.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the absence of Orco in M. hrabei.

claim: The OR gene family is the first molecular novelty (i.e. synapomorphy) for the Class Insecta.
source: Finally, we note that while insects are defined by many morphological and developmental novelties, to the best of our knowledge the OR gene family is the first molecular novelty (i.e. synapomorphy) for the Class Insecta.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of ORs in all insects but not in non-insect hexapods.

claim: The T. domestica genome assembly resulted in 618,474 scaffolds with an N50 of 15.5 Kb and a total length of 5.5 Gb.
source: The T. domestica genome assembly resulted in 618,474 scaffolds with an N50 of 15.5 Kb and a total length of 5.5 Gb.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome assembly statistics.

claim: The T. domestica genome assembly exceeds the estimated genome size of 4.6 Gb by about 1 Gb.
source: This exceeds the estimated genome size of 4.6 Gb by about 1 Gb.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of assembly size to genome size estimate.

claim: K-mer analysis revealed a high level of heterozygosity in the T. domestica sequencing data.
source: Indeed, our k-mer analysis revealed a high level of heterozygosity in the sequencing data, as indicated by the presence of a heterozygous peak of about twice the size of the homozygous peak (Supplementaryfile 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by k-mer frequency analysis.

claim: BUSCO analysis suggested a low level of gene duplication in the T. domestica genome assembly.
source: Despite the high level of heterozygosity in the sequencing data, BUSCO analysis suggested a low level of gene duplication. Only 7% of all 1066 benchmark genes tested were duplicated.
evidence: This claim is supported by BUSCO analysis results.

claim: 90.8% of the BUSCO genes were present in the T. domestica assembly, 63.6% of which were complete, and 27.2% incomplete.
source: In total, 90.8% of the BUSCO genes were present in the assembly, 63.6% of which were complete, and 27.2% incomplete.
evidence: This claim is supported by BUSCO analysis results.

claim: The T. domestica genome assembly is fragmented but likely contains the majority of all genes at least in part.
source: Although this suggests that the genome assembly is fragmented, it likely contains the majority of all genes at least in part.
evidence: This claim is inferred from BUSCO analysis results.

claim: RepeatModeler analysis identified a total of 1812 repeat element families in the T. domestica assembly, most of which could not be classified into known TE families (65.7%).
source: The RepeatModeler analysis identified a total of 1812 repeat element families in the assembly, most of which could not be classified into known TE families (65.7%).
evidence: This claim is supported by RepeatModeler analysis results.

claim: RepeatMasker annotated 9,986,807 individual elements with a cumulative length of 2.9 Gb in the T. domestica assembly, representing about half of the entire assembly length (52.9%).
source: We used the newly detected repeat elements as input database for RepeatMasker and annotated 9,986,807 individual elements with a cumulative length of 2.9 Gb, representing about half of the entire assembly length (52.9%).
evidence: This claim is supported by RepeatMasker analysis results.

claim: The T. domestica genome is highly repetitive.
source: This suggests that the genome is highly repetitive.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the high proportion of repetitive elements in the assembly.

claim: The bristletail Machilis hrabei genome encodes 5 ORs.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of all ORs we annotated in the bristletail Machilis hrabei (5 ORs), the dragonfly Ladona fulva (4 ORs), and the mayfly Ephemera danica (47 ORs), as well as the previously annotated damselfly C. splendens (6 ORs; Ioannidis et al., 2017) revealed that one of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects (Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation.

claim: The dragonfly Ladona fulva genome encodes 4 ORs.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of all ORs we annotated in the bristletail Machilis hrabei (5 ORs), the dragonfly Ladona fulva (4 ORs), and the mayfly Ephemera danica (47 ORs), as well as the previously annotated damselfly C. splendens (6 ORs; Ioannidis et al., 2017) revealed that one of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects (Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation.

claim: The mayfly Ephemera danica genome encodes 47 ORs.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of all ORs we annotated in the bristletail Machilis hrabei (5 ORs), the dragonfly Ladona fulva (4 ORs), and the mayfly Ephemera danica (47 ORs), as well as the previously annotated damselfly C. splendens (6 ORs; Ioannidis et al., 2017) revealed that one of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects (Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation.

claim: The damselfly C. splendens genome encodes 6 ORs.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of all ORs we annotated in the bristletail Machilis hrabei (5 ORs), the dragonfly Ladona fulva (4 ORs), and the mayfly Ephemera danica (47 ORs), as well as the previously annotated damselfly C. splendens (6 ORs; Ioannidis et al., 2017) revealed that one of the T. domestica ORs (TdomOrco2) clustered confidently with the Orco lineage in pterygote insects (Figure 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ioannidis et al., 2017.

claim: The genomes of all neopteran insects analyzed to date encode ORs, ranging from 10 ORs in head lice to more than 300 ORs in ants.
source: The genomes of all neopteran insects analyzed to date encode ORs, ranging from 10 ORs in head lice (Kirkness et al., 2010) to more than 300 ORs in ants (Smith et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kirkness et al., 2010 and Smith et al., 2011a, 2011b, and shown in Figure 1.

claim: TdomOrco is at least 55 kb long.
source: Thus, Orco is at least 55 kb long, Or1 is at least 14 kb long, and Or9 is at least 38 kb long.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: TdomOr1 is at least 14 kb long.
source: Thus, Orco is at least 55 kb long, Or1 is at least 14 kb long, and Or9 is at least 38 kb long.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: TdomOr9 is at least 38 kb long.
source: Thus, Orco is at least 55 kb long, Or1 is at least 14 kb long, and Or9 is at least 38 kb long.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: The T. domestica genome assembly is often redundant for two OR haplotypes.
source: These searches also revealed that our genome assembly is often redundant for two OR haplotypes, presumably resulting from the majority of the sequence being generated from a single diploid individual of high heterozygosity (described above).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of highly similar duplicate sequences in the assembly.

claim: Four T. domestica OR genes are modeled as being alternatively-spliced involving multiple long first exons in tandem array that are alternatively spliced into the four short exons encoding the C-terminus.
source: Four of these genes are modeled as being alternatively-spliced in a fashion seen commonly in insect genomes, including the original descriptions of this family from D. melanogaster (Clyne et al., 1999; Vosshall et al., 1999). This alternative splicing is somewhat unusual because it involves multiple long first exons in tandem array that are alternatively spliced into the four short exons encoding the C-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis and comparison to D. melanogaster.

claim: The alternatively-spliced T. domestica OR genes are Or15a-c, 24a/b, 27a-d, and Or31a-f.
source: These genes are Or15a-c, 24a/b, 27a-d, and Or31a-f (Table S2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: Two of the alternatively-spliced isoforms are apparent pseudogenes (Or15c and Or24b), each with single stop codons in the first long exon.
source: Two of the alternatively-spliced isoforms are apparent pseudogenes (Or15c and Or24b), each with single stop codons in the first long exon, but it is possible that these are pseudo-pseudogenes, as shown for some OR genes in Drosophila flies (Prieto-Godino et al., 2016), otherwise the remaining 41 proteins appear to be functional.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and comparison to Drosophila.

claim: The four OR models for L. fulva are full-length and intact.
source: The four OR models including Orco for L. fulva are full-length and intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation.

claim: For E. danica, in addition to Orco there are 46 OR models, 7 of which are partial models with termini or internal regions missing due to gaps in the assembly, while 10 are pseudogenes.
source: For E. danica, in addition to Orco there are 46 OR models, 7 of which are partial models with termini or internal regions missing due to gaps in the assembly that could not be repaired with raw genome reads from the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), while 10 are pseudogenes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation.

claim: All five M. hrabei OR models required considerable repairs of both ambiguous bases and assembly gaps using raw genome reads from the SRA, and three were joined across scaffolds.
source: The bristletail genome from the i5k pilot project is not available in the Apollo browser, so models for the five OR genes in that draft genome sequence were manually built in a text editor. All five required considerable repairs of both ambiguous bases and assembly gaps using raw genome reads from the SRA, and three were joined across scaffolds (Table S3 in Supplementaryfile 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genome annotation methods.

claim: There is considerable RNAseq support for four of the five M. hrabei OR models from the whole-body RNAseq of the i5k and 1Kite projects.
source: There is considerable RNAseq support for four of these five models from the whole-body RNAseq of the i5k and 1Kite projects (found with MEGABLAST searches at the SRA at NCBI), as well as five matching reads for MhraOr1 from the RNAseq of the related species employed by Missbach et al. (2014), Lepismachilis y-signata, detected using TBLASTN searches of raw reads downloaded from the SRA (Table S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome data analysis.

claim: The first two pairs of MhraOr genes are in inverse orientation to each other, with their tails adjacent.
source: We note that the first two pairs of these MhraOr genes are in inverse orientation to each other, with their tails adjacent (Table S3 in Supplementary file 1), a feature also seen with some of the TdomOrs, although they also have some genes in the head-to-head orientation, for example Orco/Or5, Or10/25, Or11/12/22, and Or13/14 (Table S2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure and genomic location analysis.

claim: There are no obvious matches for any part of Orco in the genome assembly of M. hrabei using TBLASTN searches.
source: We made extensive efforts to identify Orco in M. hrabei and L. y-signata using TdomOrco as query. There are no obvious matches for any part of Orco in the genome assembly of M. hrabei using TBLASTN searches.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' BLAST search results.

claim: TBLASTN search of raw genome reads from M. hrabei found nothing matching Orco.
source: It is always possible that a gene might be completely unassembled in a draft genome assembly, although unlikely given we were able to assemble full-length models for MhraOr1-5, so we undertook a TBLASTN search of a set of raw genome reads that gave 5-10X coverage for MhraOr1-5 and found nothing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' BLAST search results.

claim: TBLASTN searches of the raw whole-body RNAseq reads from both the i5k M. hrabei project and the 1Kite set found no Orco.
source: We also did TBLASTN searches of the raw whole-body RNAseq reads from both the i5k M. hrabei project and the 1Kite set without success.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' BLAST search results.

claim: In TBLASTN searches of the raw reads from the antennal RNAseq of Missbach et al. (2014) for L. y-signata, several reads that encode an Orco protein were found and assembled into a 713 bp contig encoding 237 amino acids, but it is a contaminant with matches of 85% identity to various lepidopteran Orco proteins.
source: Finally, in other insects Orco is generally well expressed in antennae and in TBLASTN searches of the raw reads from the antennal RNAseq of Missbach et al. (2014) for L. y-signata we found several reads that encode an Orco protein and were able to assemble a 713 bp contig encoding 237 amino acids, however it is a contaminant with matches of 85% identity to various lepidopteran Orco proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' BLAST search and sequence analysis results.

claim: The two bristletails M. hrabei and L. y-signata do not have an Orco gene.
source: We therefore conclude that these two bristletails do not have an Orco gene.
evidence: This claim is inferred from extensive unsuccessful searches for Orco in genomic and transcriptomic data.

claim: The five MhraOr genes have the same gene structure as the TdomOr9-31 genes, without the additional phase-0 intron splitting the long first exon seen in TdomOrco and the Orco-like TdomOr1-8.
source: It is also noteworthy that the five MhraOr genes have the same gene structure as the TdomOr9-31 genes, without the additional phase-0 intron splitting the long first exon seen in TdomOrco and the Orco-like TdomOr1-8 (Table S3 in Supplementary file 1), so there is no hint of Orco-like genes in this bristletail genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene structure analysis.

claim: No evidence of either Orco or ORs was found in the draft genome assemblies for three Collembola as well as a dipluran from the i5k pilot project, Catajapyx aquinolaris.
source: We similarly exhaustively examined the draft genome assemblies for three Collembola (Faddeeva-Vakhrusheva et al., 2016, 2017; Wu et al., 2017) as well as a dipluran from the i5k pilot project, Catajapyx aquinolaris, and found no evidence of either Orco or ORs, in agreement with Wu et al. (2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' genomic analysis and agrees with Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Figure 1 shows the number of ORs and OR co-receptors (Orcos) for all species of the insect and other hexapod orders analyzed mapped on the hexapod phylogeny.
source: The number of ORs and OR co-receptors (Orcos) for all species of the insect and other hexapod orders analyzed was mapped on the hexapod phylogeny sensu (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim describes the content of Figure 1.

claim: ORs are present in all insects but absent from non-insect hexapod genomes, and thus likely represent an evolutionary novelty for the Class Insecta.
source: ORs are present in all insects but absent from non-insect hexapod genomes, and thus likely represent an evolutionary novelty for the Class Insecta.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by the data shown in the figure.

claim: Orco is present in all insects analyzed except Archaeognatha.
source: Orco is present in all but Archaeognatha, an ancestrally wingless (apterygote) insect order.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Figure 1 caption and supported by the data shown in the figure.

claim: The absence of Orco in Archaeognatha suggests two scenarios including either the loss of Orco in Archaeognatha or an Orco origin following the evolution of ORs.
source: This suggests two scenarios including either the loss of Orco in Archaeognatha or an Orco origin following the evolution of ORs (as indicated).
evidence: This claim is stated in the Figure 1 caption and represents inference from the phylogenetic distribution.

claim: Figure 2 demonstrates monophyly of the single-copy insect Orco with high bootstrap support.
source: The Maximum Likelihood tree demonstrates monophyly of the single-copy insect Orco with high bootstrap support.
evidence: This claim describes the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The M. hrabei genome lacks Orco but encodes five ORs clustering in a single highly-supported clade.
source: The M. hrabei genome lacks Orco but encodes five ORs clustering in a single highly-supported clade.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Figure 2 caption and shown in the phylogenetic tree.

claim: T. domestica has a fully developed functional OR/Orco system.
source: T. domestica has a fully developed functional OR/Orco system.
evidence: This claim is stated in the Figure 2 caption and supported by the phylogenetic analysis.
